question:
Patient note:
A 35-year-old woman arrived to clinic for review of worsening fatigue, easy bruising, and vague upper-abdominal discomfort that have progressed over the past month, seeking advice prior to her next scheduled hematology appointment. She was originally diagnosed two years ago with chronic myeloid leukemia after routine blood work identified a white-cell count above 90 × 10⁹/L and a peripheral smear demonstrating a full spectrum of myeloid precursors; BCR-ABL positivity was confirmed by quantitative PCR, and she has been maintained on daily imatinib since then with good molecular response but persistent mild anemia. Over the last eight weeks she has noticed new purpura on her forearms after minimal trauma and feels more winded climbing a single flight of stairs than earlier in the year, prompting today’s visit with her primary internist. Eight years earlier she was found to have symmetric polyarthritis of the small joints of the hands accompanied by intermittent photosensitive malar rash and low-titer anti-dsDNA antibodies; hydroxychloroquine 200 mg twice daily has largely controlled joint flares, and a brief course of prednisone six months ago for pleuritic chest pain was the last time she required systemic steroids. Four years ago she was hospitalized for melena and received two units of packed red cells; upper endoscopy revealed a 1.5-cm clean-based duodenal ulcer and she was discharged on twice-daily pantoprazole, which she continues. She denies any subsequent hematemesis, but reports occasional epigastric burning when she misses doses of her acid suppressant. There has been no prior history of myocardial infarction, coronary revascularization, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, orthopnea, or ankle swelling, and she jogs three miles three times weekly without chest tightness. She has never experienced unilateral weakness, aphasia, facial droop, or visual field cuts suggestive of cerebral ischemia, and neurologic review of systems is otherwise unremarkable. Cognition remains sharp; she is in graduate school and maintains a 4.0 GPA while also coordinating her own complex medication schedule. She has never used tobacco, drinks wine socially once or twice per month, and denies recreational drug use. There is no personal or family history of chronic lung disease, and she has had no wheeze, chronic cough, or dyspnea outside of her recent fatigue. She follows a Mediterranean diet and has never carried a diagnosis of abnormal glucose tolerance; a fasting serum glucose performed two weeks ago during leukemia surveillance labs was 94 mg/dL, and she has never required antihyperglycemic therapy. Previous comprehensive metabolic panels have shown normal alanine aminotransferase, alkaline phosphatase, and total bilirubin; hepatitis B surface antigen and hepatitis C antibody are negative, and she has no stigmata of chronic liver dysfunction on exam. Renal function has remained normal with creatinine 0.7 mg/dL and estimated GFR >90 mL/min/1.73 m², and urinalysis is without proteinuria or hematuria. She has no personal history of solid organ malignancy, and her most recent Pap smear was negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy. HIV antibody/antigen testing last year was non-reactive. Surgical history is limited to wisdom tooth extraction. Current medications include imatinib, hydroxychloroquine, pantoprazole, calcium carbonate with vitamin D, and a combined oral contraceptive; she takes no NSAIDs chronically because of concern for gastrointestinal bleeding. Review of systems is negative for fevers, drenching night sweats, or unintentional weight loss. On arrival today she appeared pale but in no acute distress. Vital signs: temperature 36.9 °C, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, heart rate 98 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 98 % breathing room air, body mass index 24 kg/m². Conjunctival pallor was present, sclera anicteric. Cardiac examination revealed a regular rhythm without murmurs, gallops, or rubs; jugular venous pressure was not elevated. Lungs were clear to auscultation without crackles or wheezes. Abdomen was soft with mild epigastric tenderness but no guarding, rebound, or organomegaly. There were several 1–2 cm nontender cervical lymph nodes felt to be reactive. No pedal edema was observed. Neurologic exam showed intact cranial nerves, 5/5 strength throughout, normal sensation, and brisk symmetrical reflexes. Skin inspection identified scattered petechiae and ecchymoses on the forearms and shins without palpable purpura. Laboratory studies drawn this morning revealed hemoglobin 8.9 g/dL, platelets 78 × 10⁹/L, white-cell count 38 × 10⁹/L with myelocytes and metamyelocytes, creatinine 0.8 mg/dL, AST 22 U/L, ALT 18 U/L, total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL, and international normalized ratio 1.1. Given the constellation of worsening cytopenias, prior history of autoimmune connective tissue involvement, and remote bleeding from an upper-gastrointestinal ulcer, she was advised to coordinate urgent follow-up with hematology for bone marrow evaluation while arrangements were made for repeat upper endoscopy to assess mucosal healing before any potential intensification of leukemia therapy.

Question: What is the patient's Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) sums the weights of qualifying baseline conditions.
- Chronic myeloid leukemia: 2 points for leukemia, even with a good response to imatinib.
- Connective tissue disease: 1 point for the lupus history supported by inflammatory polyarthritis, malar rash, and anti-dsDNA antibodies.
- Peptic ulcer disease: 1 point for the endoscopically confirmed bleeding duodenal ulcer.
- Age 35: 0 age-adjustment points. No other qualifying condition is documented; anemia and thrombocytopenia are not separate CCI items.
Total: 2 + 1 + 1 + 0 = 4.
Final answer: 4
